newsitem.title: ITALY: FORECAST- Italy February CPI seen at 2.5 pct y/y.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST- Italy February CPI seen at 2.5 pct y/y.

text.p: Italy's inflation should continue slowing in February due to stagnating domestic demand and extraordinary factors such as a fall in meat prices and electricity bills, a Reuter poll of 14 analysts showed.

On average, economists see year on year inflation falling to 2.5 percent from 2.6 percent in January. Monthly inflation should stay flat from January at 0.2 percent. The range for monthly inflation was 0.1-0.3 percent.
In February 1996 the consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.3 percent month-on-month and 5.0 percent year-on-year.

"Inflation expectations are under control. The fall in the yearly rate will continue and CPI will touch a nadir in May, when it will be under 2.0 percent, but will then start rising again," Paolo Casadio, economist at Credito Italiano said.
Other analysts noted weakness in internal demand prevented producers from passing production price rises on to consumers.
On Thursday and Friday 11 sample Italian cities will publish their consumer prices data for February. National statistics body Istat releases the final national figure on March 4.

Analysts attributed an expected slight fall in year on year CPI to food and tariffs but noted there could be some gains in durable goods prices while labour and leisure sector costs should remain stable.
"The positive effect of the cut in value added tax on meat (from 16 percent to 10 percent) on January 1 will continue," Rodolfo Dozio, economist at Banca Commerciale Italiana said.
"The impact of this was not entirely carried on the January data because the smaller stores have slow price adjustment procedures," Dozio added.

State electricity group Enel announced Thursday that it would reduce electricity bills to rescind price rises passed in 1993. Analysts said this fall could have a positive impact of around 0.03 percent in February.
"The Enel price cut is not high, but it's an extra factor which could help reduce the yearly rate," BCI said.
Other tariffs remained stable this month, with the price hike on railway tickets effective only in March.

"The metalworkers' contract is very favourable. It should not cause any tension on labour costs because the salary hikes will be counterbalanced by an increase in production, after a period of lower productivity," Pio de Gregorio, analyst at NatWest in Milan said.
Any possible tension could derive from the stronger dollar which could impact on PPI and eventually also on CPI.
"For the time being, in the production phase, the impact has been limited but these types of pressures must be kept under control," Casadio of Credito Italiano said.
